questions.question: What is the main problem that semantic chunking tries to solve?
options: It is faster than fixed-size chunking
It keeps related content together along meaning boundaries instead of cutting at an arbitrary character count
It removes the need for embeddings
It guarantees better ranking on every query
questions.explanation: Fixed-size chunking cuts mid-sentence and can separate a question from its answer. Semantic chunking splits on meaning boundaries so a chunk is more likely to be coherent on its own — at the cost of slower, less predictable indexing.

questions.question: What does an embedding represent?
options: A summary of the text in natural language
A vector of numbers that places text with similar meaning close together
The keywords found in the text, in order
A compressed copy of the original text
questions.explanation: An embedding maps text to a point in a high-dimensional space. Texts that mean similar things land near each other, which is what makes similarity search work.

questions.question: Which are reasons to store metadata alongside each chunk? Select all that apply.
options: To filter retrieval by document, section or date before searching
To give the model a citation and a way to verify the answer
To make every chunk the same length
To allow hard filtering — for example, only searching one product line
questions.explanation: Metadata turns a bag of vectors into a searchable library: it filters, it cites, and it scopes the search. It does not change the length of a chunk.

questions.question: The larger the chunk, the better the retrieval, because the model gets more context.
questions.explanation: False. Large chunks dilute the embedding — the vector now describes several ideas at once — and push more irrelevant text into the prompt. There is a sweet spot, and it depends on the embedding model and the question set.

questions.question: Two chunks have cosine similarity 0.92. What does that say about them?
questions.answer: Their embeddings point in nearly the same direction, so they are likely to be about similar things
questions.explanation: Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors. 1.0 means identical direction, 0 means unrelated. 0.92 is high, so the chunks are semantically close — but it is a ranking signal, not a guarantee of relevance.

questions.question: A chunk of 2,000 characters is split so that the last 200 characters of one chunk are repeated at the start of the next. What is this for?
options: To make the chunks compress better
To stop a sentence being cut in half and lost across the boundary
To reduce the number of chunks stored
To speed up the embedding call
questions.explanation: That overlap is the usual fix for boundary loss: if a sentence straddles the cut, the overlap keeps enough of it inside both chunks that at least one of them can answer a question about it.
